title: Delta Air Lines 9570
summary: Delta Flight 9570, a DC-9 training flight with four occupants including an FAA inspector, was cleared to land behind an American DC-10 at Greater Southwest International Airport. The aircraft received an advisory about turbulence but was not explicitly advised it was following a heavy aircraft. On approach, the DC-9 began to oscillate about the roll axis, then rolled rapidly to the right, striking the runway with its wingtip and continuing to roll until the fuselage struck in a nearly inverted position. All four occupants were killed and the aircraft was destroyed.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined that the accident was caused by wake turbulence from the DC-10 that the DC-9 had followed. NTSB wake vortex testing at Atlantic City Airport demonstrated that wake turbulence from a DC-10 was sufficient to upset a following DC-9 to the magnitude experienced. The accident led to sweeping changes in procedures for maintaining safe distance behind large aircraft generating substantial wake turbulence.

factors.evidence: The air traffic controller did not advise the DC-9 crew that they were following a heavy aircraft, though the controller advised they were following a DC-10 which experienced pilots should have known was a heavy aircraft

Prior to Flight 9570, most accidents involving wake turbulence involved smaller aircraft than the DC-9, suggesting crews had not been trained to recognize wake turbulence hazard to larger twin-engine aircraft from heavy jets

The DC-9 began to oscillate about the roll axis, then rolled rapidly to the right, with the right wingtip striking the runway and the aircraft continuing to roll until the fuselage struck the runway in a nearly inverted position

title: British European Airways 548
summary: Hawker Siddeley Trident entered a deep stall during initial climb shortly after takeoff from Heathrow and descended steeply until crashing near Staines. The aircraft had not achieved sufficient airspeed and high-lift devices were not properly configured for the climb phase. The public inquiry principally blamed the captain for failing to maintain airspeed and configure the aircraft correctly. The captain had an undiagnosed heart condition and the co-pilot had limited experience. The aircraft's T-tail design and high-lift system made it vulnerable to deep stall if airspeed was insufficient and high-lift devices were not extended.
probable_cause: The captain failed to maintain sufficient airspeed and failed to extend high-lift devices properly during initial climb, causing the aircraft to enter a deep stall from which recovery was impossible. The captain's undiagnosed heart condition may have contributed to impaired judgment. An unspecified technical problem apparently resolved before takeoff and limited co-pilot experience with the aircraft also contributed to the accident.

title: 1972 Lake Winnebago mid-air collision

aircraft.type: Convair CV-580 and de Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter

operator: North Central Airlines and Air Wisconsin
summary: North Central Flight 290 (CV-580) and Air Wisconsin Flight 671 (DHC-6 Twin Otter) collided in mid-air over Lake Winnebago at 2,500 feet in bright sunshine with scattered clouds. The collision tore off portions of both aircraft's wings, rendering them uncontrollable. Both crashed into the lake. The NTSB determined that both crews failed to detect the other aircraft visually in sufficient time to take evasive action, a failure attributed to atmospheric conditions, human visual limitations, and crews possibly scanning instruments for descent preparation rather than maintaining surveillance for traffic.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from the failure of both flight crews to detect visually the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. The ability to detect each other was reduced by atmospheric conditions and human visual limitations. The decision by both crews to fly VFR rather than IFR deprived both aircraft of air traffic control support that would have ensured adequate separation.

factors.evidence: The left wing of Flight 671 hit the left wing of Flight 290 at 2,500 feet, resulting in an explosion that tore off most of the Twin Otter's wing and about a quarter of the CV-580's left wing.
Both flight crews failed to detect visually the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action.
The NTSB speculated that both flight crews could have been scanning instruments in preparation for descent to their respective destinations at the time of the collision.

Neither aircraft had access to air traffic control radar separation because both crews chose to operate under VFR rather than IFR, a procedural choice enabled by VFR rules that do not mandate ATC coordination.

title: Interflug 450

title: Aeroflot 217
summary: Aeroflot Flight 217 was flying at 1200 m when ATC cleared descent to 400 m. The crew confirmed and started to descend normally, but the aircraft failed to level off and passed the 400 m mark at 20 m/s descent rate with engines at low thrust. The aircraft crashed with landing gear up and spoilers retracted. Investigators concluded that the probable cause was psycho-physiological incapacitation of the crew.

title: 1972 Andes flight disaster
summary: A Fairchild FH-227D carrying 45 members of a Uruguayan rugby team and their relatives crashed in the Andes Mountains on 13 October 1972, killing 31 occupants. The inexperienced co-pilot Dante Lagurara, while being trained by experienced Captain Ferradas, mistakenly believed the aircraft had passed the Curicó turning point when it was still 37 kilometers east of that position. The crew initiated descent prematurely in instrument meteorological conditions with cloud cover obscuring the terrain, causing the aircraft to strike a mountain ridge at 12,020 feet, shearing off both wings and the tail cone.
probable_cause: Navigation error by the co-pilot who misjudged the aircraft position while in cloud, leading to premature descent and collision with mountainous terrain.

title: Japan Airlines 446
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 446, a Douglas DC-8-62, crashed 30 seconds after takeoff from Sheremetyevo when the aircraft stalled at 100 meters altitude. The copilot accidentally deployed ground spoilers by selecting the wrong lever, and the No. 2 engine experienced thrust loss, likely from icing as engine anti-ice was not activated despite winter conditions. When the captain pulled the nose up excessively to compensate for poor climb performance, the aircraft stalled and became uncontrollable.
probable_cause: The aircraft stalled on takeoff due to reduced performance from accidental ground spoiler deployment and asymmetric engine thrust. The crew did not have engine anti-ice activated despite winter conditions. The subsequent excessive nose-up input deepened the stall.

title: United Air Lines 553
summary: A Boeing 737 approaching Chicago Midway was too high on descent at the outer marker beacon. The captain extended spoilers and steepened descent to 1,550 feet per minute, well above the normal 1,000 fpm. After leveling at minimum descent altitude with engines not advanced fully and spoilers still extended, the aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall. The stick shaker activated and continued sounding until impact into a residential neighborhood. The flight data recorder was inoperative due to maintenance failure.

title: 1972 Chicago-O'Hare runway collision
summary: North Central Airlines Flight 575 collided with Delta Air Lines Flight 954 on a runway at O'Hare during takeoff in foggy conditions with visibility of one-quarter mile. The NTSB found the probable cause was failure of the traffic control system to ensure adequate aircraft separation due to an ambiguous holding clearance and misunderstood ground control instructions. Ten passengers on the DC-9 died in a post-collision fire.

title: Braathens SAFE 239
summary: The Fokker F28 crashed during approach to Oslo after the pilots took a shortcut and turned too early due to ILS system deviations. Combined with false signals from the instrument landing system and confusion about their position, the aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck terrain near Asker. The investigation found navigational error was the probable cause, with the ILS known to deviate up to twenty-five degrees under certain conditions.

title: Eastern Air Lines 401
summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 401 crashed in the Florida Everglades shortly before midnight after the autopilot inadvertently disconnected. A subtle bump of the yoke switched the autopilot from altitude hold to Control Wheel Steering mode. While the crew was focused on a malfunctioning landing gear indicator light, they did not notice the autopilot disconnection and the aircraft gradually lost altitude until striking the ground.
probable_cause: A subtle bump of the yoke caused the autopilot to switch from altitude hold mode to Control Wheel Steering mode. The crew's focus on a malfunctioning landing gear indicator light distracted them from noticing the altitude loss.

title: 1972 Puerto Rico DC-7 crash
summary: On December 31, 1972, a Douglas DC-7CF cargo aircraft crashed immediately after takeoff from San Juan, Puerto Rico, killing all five on board including baseball legend Roberto Clemente. The aircraft was overweight and the No. 2 engine failed after takeoff due to inadequate maintenance following a taxiway accident 29 days earlier. The pilot was attempting to return to the airport when the aircraft descended into the ocean near Piñones.
probable_cause: The NTSB concluded that after the failure of the No. 2 engine, inadequate maintenance contributed to the accident. Following an earlier taxiway accident that damaged the propeller blades and engine cooler scoop, the standard procedure to magnaflux the engine for cracks was not performed. The aircraft also was three percent overweight at takeoff.
